title: Smash Burger
kicker: A ball of beef, a spatula, and the physics of maximum crust. The burger that out-burgered the gourmet burger.
story: The smash burger reverses everything the burger purists told you. Do not handle the meat gently. Do not keep it thick. Do press it — hard — into a screaming hot griddle, where the flattened patty develops a deep brown crust (the Maillard reaction's greatest hits album) in under two minutes. The lacy, caramelized edges are the entire point.

Two rules make it work. First: 80/20 beef, formed into loose balls and seasoned only on the outside — salting early changes the texture. Second: do not press after the first minute. Smash once, hard, with a stiff spatula, then leave it alone while the crust forms. Thin patties mean you stack two for the classic double, and double sauce dripping down your wrist is the standard unit of success.
fun_fact: The technique traces to Smoky's, a 1930s Wisconsin stand, and was revived by Denver's Smashburger chain and LA's In-N-Out cult. The spatula you use matters so much that dedicated 'smashers' are now sold.

steps.title: Form balls, not patties
steps.text: Divide beef into 8 loose 100 g balls. Do not compress. Do not season yet. They should look like they were rolled by someone in a hurry.

steps.title: Nuclear preheat
steps.text: Cast-iron griddle or heavy skillet on high for 5 minutes until it hisses at a water drop. This is the difference between burger and burger-shaped gray meat.

steps.title: Smash, once, hard
steps.text: Two balls per bun. Place on the griddle, smash flat with a stiff spatula (use a second spatula or a can to press) to 5 mm. Salt and pepper now. Never touch it again for 2 minutes.

steps.title: Crust, flip, cheese
steps.text: When the edges are dark and lacy and the top is still red-pink, flip once — crust down is what you cooked for. Immediately lay cheese on, stack the second patty on top of the first's melted cheese.

steps.title: Toast the buns in the fat
steps.text: Butter the cut sides and press them onto the griddle during the patties' final minute. Golden, steaming, slightly greasy — correct.

steps.title: Build fast, eat faster
steps.text: Sauce on both bun halves, pickles, onions, double patty. Wrap half the burger in paper if you want the authentic grip. The whole thing from skillet to mouth should take under 60 seconds.

notes: American cheese is functionally correct here — it melts. If you must be fancy, grate your cheddar fine and accept less ooze.
A metal bench scraper lifts the crusty patties cleanly off the griddle.
No griddle? The biggest cast-iron skillet works; just cook two patties at a time and keep the heat brutal.

storage: Smash burgers are a now-food. Leftover cooked patties keep 2 days and re-crisp in a skillet — but honestly, form the extra balls instead and smash fresh.

equipment.n: flat-top substitute; pre-heat until it just smokes
stiff, metal - you will smash with it
the flip-and-scrape trick keeps the crust on the patty

facts.first_recorded: 2000s — the crust became the point; the Smashburger brand arrived 2007 and the style went national
facts.name_means: Named after the verb. The whole technique is in the smash.
facts.technique: Maillard maximization: smash thin, scrape, flip once
facts.season: Any — it is diner food, diners have no season
facts.signature: Lacy beef crust, melted American, steam-softened onions
facts.serve_at: In the paper wrapper, slightly crushed on purpose
facts.pour: A vanilla milkshake — the correct answer

similar.n: crust is the point — both fried in their own fat
